scenes.text: Last video ended with two curves. Both follow x squared, up to x equals one. The first carries on along its tangent, y equals two x minus one, and the second along y equals x. Let's turn them into skate tracks. Roll a skateboard down the first, and it passes the join without a bump. On the second, it jolts, because the track's angle changes all at once. Both tracks are unbroken, with no gaps. Now zoom in on each join. The first straightens out into a single line. The second stays a corner, however far you zoom. So what does a join need, for the curve to have a gradient there?

Here's the test. Take the point P, at x equals a, and a nearby point Q, a small step h along. The gradient of the line through them is f of a plus h, minus f of a, all over h. You met that in Year 11. Now shrink h towards zero, from the right, and also from the left, because h can be negative. If those gradients settle on one finite number, from both sides, f is differentiable at a. That number is f prime of a, and the curve has a single tangent there that isn't vertical. If they don't settle, there's no derivative at a.

Try it on the first join, at x equals one. From the right, Q is on the line y equals two x minus one, so every secant gradient is exactly two. From the left, Q is on x squared, and the gradient is two plus h. So, one point five, one point nine, one point nine nine, heading to two. Both sides settle on two. So this function is differentiable at one, with f prime of one equal to two. The line is the tangent to x squared, so both pieces leave the join in the same direction. That's why the board doesn't jolt.

Now the second join, where the right piece is y equals x. From the left, nothing changes. The gradients still head to two. But from the right, every secant gradient is exactly one. Two from one side, one from the other. There's no single number, so there's no derivative at x equals one. The curve is unbroken, but it isn't differentiable there. That's what a corner is: two different one-sided gradients. On the track, that's the jolt, from forty-five degrees to about sixty-three, in an instant.

What if the gradients match, but the pieces don't meet? Here, x squared runs up to one, one. Then the right piece is y equals two x, which starts at height two. On a track, that's a step. Its gradient is two, the same as x squared at the join. A function is continuous at a when, from both sides, the curve heads to the value f of a itself. Here, from the right it heads to two, but f of one is one. So it isn't continuous. Now look at the secant from P, to a point on the right piece. The rise never drops below one, while the run shrinks to zero. So the gradient blows up, to twelve, then a hundred and two, and beyond. No derivative. This is why a function that's differentiable at a point must be continuous there. If the gradients settle on a finite number, the rise is that gradient times the run. So the rise shrinks to zero with the run, and the curve can't jump.

There's one more way to fail, even with no join at all. Take y equals the cube root of x, at zero. It's unbroken, and it looks smooth. But the secant gradients are h to the power minus two thirds. They grow without limit from both sides, because the tangent at the origin is vertical. A board there would point straight up. A vertical tangent has no gradient, so the cube root of x isn't differentiable at zero. That's why the definition says a tangent that isn't vertical. At a cusp, a sharp point where both sides arrive steeply, the gradients blow up in opposite directions. So there's no derivative there either.

So at a join, check two things, in order. First, do the pieces meet? Compare the value at the join with the height the other piece heads to. If they don't meet, stop. It's not differentiable. Second, do the gradients match? Each piece here is smooth on its own side, so differentiate each one, and evaluate both at the join. Equal gradients mean differentiable. Different gradients mean a corner. Continuity on its own isn't enough.

Now a worked example. h of x is x squared for x up to two, and a x plus b for x greater than two. Find a and b so that h is differentiable at two. Match the gradients first. x squared has gradient two x, which is four at x equals two. The line's gradient is a. So a equals four. Now make the pieces meet. At x equals two, x squared is four, and the line gives two a plus b. So four equals eight plus b, and b is minus four. The line is y equals four x minus four, the tangent to x squared at two, so a board rolls through without a jolt. You need both equations. The gradient alone leaves b free, and the join could still jump.

A short way to hold it: meet, then match. The pieces meet, so there's no step, and the function is continuous. The gradients match, so there's no kink, and it's differentiable. Meeting alone isn't enough.

Your turn. g of x is three minus x squared, for x up to and including one, and x plus one, for x greater than one. Is g continuous at x equals one? Is it differentiable there? Justify both answers. Pause here to answer.

x equals one belongs to the first piece, so g of one is three minus one, which is two. The second piece heads to one plus one, also two. They meet, so g is continuous. The gradients are minus two x, which is minus two, and one. Minus two isn't one, so g isn't differentiable at one. There's a corner, at one, two. Being continuous doesn't make it differentiable.

Last one. f of x is e to the two x, for x up to and including zero, and a x plus b, for x greater than zero. Find the values of a and b that make f differentiable at x equals zero. Pause here to answer.

Match the gradients. The derivative of e to the two x is two e to the two x, which is two at zero. So a equals two. Now meet. e to the zero is one, and the line gives b at zero, so b equals one. The line is y equals two x plus one. Not b equals zero. Then the pieces would miss by one, and the curve would jump.

Back to the smooth join. At x equals one, both sides have gradient two. But look at how the gradient changes. On the left, it's minus one, then zero, then one, still rising as we move right.
